content: Froth flotation is a highly selective and specialized process used to separate valuable minerals from gangue by employing surfactants and wetting agents. This method enables the economic processing of complex ores, such as mixed sulfides, carbonates, and oxides, by isolating the desired minerals. Additionally, froth flotation is applied to the beneficiation of phosphates and coal. Beyond mineral processing, this technique is extensively utilized in industrial wastewater treatment to remove fats, oils, grease, and suspended solids. In such applications, the process is implemented through Dissolved Air Flotation (DAF) units, which are particularly effective in treating wastewater effluents from oil refineries, petrochemical plants, chemical facilities, and natural gas processing plants. The origins of froth flotation date back to 1869 when William Haynes patented a process for separating sulfide minerals from gangue using oil, which he termed bulk-oil flotation. The modern froth flotation process was independently developed in 1901 by C.V. Potter in Australia and in 1902 by G.D. Delprat in Holland. Initially, naturally occurring chemicals like fatty acids and oils were used as flotation reagents in large quantities. Over time, the process evolved to accommodate a broader range of materials, incorporating synthetic surfactants and collector agents for enhanced efficiency and selectivity. The operation of froth flotation begins with comminution, a process of crushing and grinding the ore to increase its surface area and liberate the desired mineral from the gangue. The ore is then ground into a fine powder. A surfactant or collector chemical is added to render the target mineral hydrophobic, while the gangue remains hydrophilic. The choice of surfactant depends on the specific mineral being processed; for instance, pine oil is commonly used in copper extraction. The resulting slurry, or pulp, is introduced into a water bath that is aerated to create bubbles. The hydrophobic mineral particles attach to the air bubbles and rise to the surface, forming a froth. This froth, enriched with the desired mineral, is skimmed off for further refinement. The effectiveness of froth flotation relies on the selective wetting properties of the surfactants used. A suitable surfactant will completely wet one type of particle while only partially wetting the other, allowing the bubbles to adhere to the desired particles and lift them into the froth. The degree of wetting can be quantified by measuring the contact angle at the liquid-bubble interface. For complete wetting, the contact angle is zero. Additionally, the buoyant forces of the bubbles must counterbalance the weight of the particles, particularly for heavier materials. The relationship between particle size, surface tension, density, and buoyancy determines whether a particle will rise into the froth layer. Froth flotation can be conducted in various types of equipment, including mechanically agitated cells, tall flotation columns, and specialized units like the Jameson cell. Mechanical cells use a mixer and diffuser mechanism to introduce air and agitate the slurry, resulting in higher throughput but lower-quality material. In contrast, flotation columns employ air spargers to introduce air at the base of a tall column, with the countercurrent motion of slurry and air providing mixing. This method produces higher-quality material but at a lower throughput rate. The mechanics of froth flotation involve several key steps. First, the ore is ground to liberate the mineral particles. Next, reagents are added to condition the slurry and impart hydrophobic surface charges to the desired particles. Air or nitrogen bubbles are then introduced, allowing the hydrophobic particles to attach and rise to the surface, forming a stable froth. This froth, enriched with the target mineral, is separated from the flotation cell for further processing. In a typical flotation circuit, the pulp is conditioned in a tank before being fed into rougher cells, where most of the desired minerals are collected as a concentrate. The remaining pulp is sent to scavenger cells for additional treatment, with the froth often recycled back to the rougher cells. More complex circuits may include cleaner and re-cleaner cells, as well as intermediate re-grinding stages. Various chemicals are used in froth flotation to optimize the process. Collectors are added to enhance the hydrophobicity of the target mineral. Frothers stabilize the froth, ensuring that it remains intact for collection. Modifiers are used to adjust the pH and influence the interaction between reagents and minerals. Common pH modifiers include lime (CaO), soda ash (Na2CO3), caustic soda (NaOH), and acids like H2SO4 and HCl. Cationic modifiers, such as Ba2+, Ca2+, Cu+, Pb2+, Zn2+, and Ag+, and anionic modifiers, like SiO32-, PO43-, CN-, CO32-, and S2-, are employed to alter the surface properties of the particles. Organic modifiers, including dextrin, starch, glue, and carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), are also used to enhance selectivity. Froth flotation is tailored to specific ore types, with reagents and equipment configurations adjusted to achieve optimal separation and recovery of valuable minerals.
